wording.proposed: Replace 'Narrative reviews describe the memory deficits as larger and more consistent (Parrott, 2011, 2013)' with: 'Narrative reviews report larger pooled differences from the same meta-analytic literature while themselves describing marked variation across individual studies, which they attribute to lifetime dose, sample size and method (Parrott, 2011, 2013).' Also repair two sentences whose missing commas make the ratings read as verbs: 'A 2026 meta-analysis, whose confidence was rated critically low, pooled four or five small studies per comparison...' and 'A 2009 review of 33 studies, also rated critically low, pooled no effect sizes and found...'.
wording.reason: 'More consistent' is the opposite of what my two sources say. Parrott (2011), p. 1365, 2nd paragraph, opens with 'marked variation across studies' and describes individual studies as a mixture of significant and non-significant results behind significant pooled estimates; Parrott (2013), p. 8 of the in-press PDF, §3.5, 5th paragraph, says that even on the tasks that often show deficits they are 'not universally apparent'. What the two do is report larger pooled effects (d -0.27 to -1.00 from Laws and Kokkalis, p. 5-6) and explain the variation, not claim consistency.

status.reason: Several studies with inconsistent findings and no adequate explanation of the heterogeneity (I2 of 94 to 96% in the pooled estimates, deficits on some tasks and not others): mixed, as METHODS §6.4 defines it. The reviews that make up most of the evidence share primary studies, so nothing here supports 'replicated'.

grade.reason: Observational start low; one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision, floor at very low. Publication bias at 0 is defensible since neither review assessed it, and the domain note says so.

verification.reason: Not narrative-only: the supporting anchors include a meta-analysis and a systematic review read in full by the other reader, so §6.3's draft rule does not bite, and metadata-verified is the right rung while the anchors are still being checked.

debate.reason: No debate box on this claim.

note: Editor's question, whether Murphy et al. (2009) is a systematic review or a narrative review: it is a systematic review by search and eligibility, so reader 24's classification and AMSTAR 2 are right. Its 'Method - Identification of Studies' (p. 160) names the databases (PsycInfo and Medline), gives 46 search terms built from the task list, dates the searches (July to September 2008) and states that no date limits were applied; 59 references were screened against stated inclusion and exclusion criteria and 33 were included (p. 161). It is unlike the narrative reviews in my half of the batch, which have no search at all. What it lacks - a protocol, duplicate screening, any risk-of-bias appraisal of the included studies and any pooling - is what AMSTAR 2 should record (items 11, 12 and 15 as 'no meta-analysis'), and critically low confidence follows from that, not from the design label.

wording.proposed: Two changes. (1) Change the relation from 'does-not-detectably-change' to 'insufficient-evidence' (or keep 'does not detectably change' only for the memory measures, whose intervals are reported). (2) Replace 'a medium one (d 0.5) on only 6 of them' with 'a medium one (d 0.5) on 5 of them, with a sixth at exactly 0.50'.
wording.reason: (1) METHODS §6.3 requires a 'no detectable effect' claim to rest on intervals that exclude meaningful effects. This study's own Table 4 leaves a medium effect in play on 8 of 14 measures, and the study did detect differences: four whole-group measures at p<.05 and, in the heavier-use subgroup, the strategy test at p=.003 with a within-group dose relation (r=-0.37). The claim's own statement says all of this, so the relation field contradicts the body. (2) Table 4's maximum excludable effects are 0.37, 0.40, 0.48, 0.49, 0.49, 0.50, 0.53, 0.54, 0.54 ... 0.76; strictly below 0.5 on five measures, with the Iowa Gambling Task at exactly 0.50, where a medium effect is not excluded.

status.reason: One study; the two commentaries in my half add no data and read the same tables in opposite ways (Parrott, 2011, p. 1366; Lyvers, 2011, 1st paragraph).

grade.reason: Low start, down for risk of bias and imprecision, very low. If the relation is changed as proposed the domains need no change.

verification.reason: Rests on a primary study read in full, with the commentaries as qualifiers; metadata-verified is right.

note: Editor's question about 'many': Halpern et al.'s Table 4 lists 14 measures with maximum excludable effect sizes from 0.37 to 0.76. A large effect (d 0.8) is excluded on all 14, a medium effect strictly on 5 and at best on 6, so 'many' in the paper's Discussion is not supported and the claim is right to give the count. I also confirmed the claim's other Halpern figures against Tables 1 to 3 in PMC3053129: four whole-group differences at p<.05 (vocabulary 0.01, digit symbol 0.02, spatial span forward 0.04, non-dominant pegboard 0.02) with Raven's and digits backwards at 0.05; strategy test 79.5 against 88.5%, difference 8.7 (3.1 to 14.4), p=.003; CVLT trials 1-5 difference -0.5 (-4.2 to 3.2); and the group differences in parental education, ethnicity, raves and cannabis.

wording.proposed: Replace the last sentence with: 'Two further prospective datasets are known here only through a narrative review (Parrott, 2013): one of them (de Win et al., 2008) reports the same Netherlands cohort as Schilt et al., the other is cited as Wagner et al. (2013) but has no entry in that review's reference list, and the review also misstates this cohort's retest interval as 18 to 36 months.'
wording.reason: 'A second prospective cohort' is ambiguous and understates the problem. At p. 6 of the in-press PDF the review describes two further prospective datasets, and at p. 5 it presents de Win et al. (2008) as a separate study although both it and Schilt et al. report the 188-person Netherlands XTC Toxicity cohort (Schilt et al., PDF pp. 728-729). The other, cited as Wagner et al. (2013), has no matching entry anywhere in the proof's reference list, so a reader cannot identify it. The retest-interval error is correctly stated as it stands (the review says 18-36 months; Schilt et al., p. 731, report 11.1 and 19.1 months).

status.reason: One cohort read in full; the others are second-hand, and one of them is the same cohort.

wording.proposed: Extend one clause: 'In a prospective cohort with very low use, binding did not differ, although other imaging measures in that cohort did and its authors wrote that they could not exclude that even low doses are neurotoxic.'
wording.reason: As it stands, 'binding did not differ' reads as a clean null. The review (p. 5 of the in-press PDF, §2.2) reports in the same breath that cerebral blood volume, fractional anisotropy and apparent diffusion differed and quotes the cohort's authors to that effect; the contradicting anchor already carries both halves, and the statement should not be narrower than its own anchor. Everything else in the statement and the magnitude matches the two sources: -19% to -46% and -21% (Parrott 2013, p. 4, and Parrott 2011, pp. 1366-1367), and -56%, -19%, -32% with no change in the hallucinogen-preferring group (Parrott 2013, p. 4).

status.reason: Mixed is right: the review itself says not every study found reductions, and the prospective cohort with very low use found none.

grade.reason: Low start, down for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness; very low, floor reached. I agree with not upgrading for the dose relationships, which are reported second-hand from the same cross-sectional samples.

wording.proposed: Two changes. (1) 'The one report that claimed it, a 2002 primate study, was retracted...' becomes 'The primate report that put the question on the agenda in 2002 was retracted...'. (2) After the critics' citations, add: 'that description does not hold for one of the studies they cite, in which the dopamine metabolite was lower in the MDMA group (McCann et al., 1994)'.
wording.reason: (1) Within the sources read, the 2002 study is not the only claim of a dopamine effect: its authors' reply also cites mouse findings of MDMA-induced dopamine neurotoxicity and their own dosing-pattern observation (p. 1504, Response, 3rd paragraph). (2) As worded, the reader meets the critics' 'normal dopamine markers' and, three sentences later, the McCann CSF figures, without being told that McCann et al. (1994) is one of the studies the critics cite (their reference 11). The card for mithoefer_2003 records this; the claim should carry it.

status.reason: Contested is workable and keeps the debate box the question needs, but it should be read with the asymmetry the box describes: after the retraction no primary evidence for the yes side is before us, so the dispute is about the interpretation of human markers rather than about two bodies of evidence.

grade.reason: Low start, down for risk of bias (partisan letters, an assertion with no human citation) and indirectness (no human dopamine measurement among the supporting sources); very low. Imprecision at 0 is right because no estimate is made.

debate.reason: Three points. (a) In 'evidence_no', the critics' statement that earlier work by the same group found CSF dopamine metabolites not reduced is presented as part of their case without the correction, which appears only two sections later; the parenthesis proposed above should be added there too, because that is where a reader forms the impression. (b) In 'editors_reading', 'no human evidence for it has been put before us' is not supportable beside the claim's own sentence that CSF HVA was lower in the MDMA group after adjustment (19.4 against 27.4 ng/ml, p=.01, carried by the women): propose 'the only human dopamine-marker finding before us is a lower metabolite in spinal fluid, clearly only in women, in a group that had used other drugs far more often, which cannot show damage'. (c) 'evidence_yes' omits that the mortality argument turns on a disputed number: the reply says one of ten animals died (p. 1504), Barnett and Doblin say two (p. 2 of the online-first PDF), and neither read the 2002 paper. Otherwise each side's strongest material is fairly stated from my sources, and the dosing-pattern argument is reported accurately.

debate.reason: The yes side is fairly stated from parrott_2013, parrott_2011 and cowan_2012, and I found nothing in it that those sources do not say. Three changes on the other side and in the editors' reading. (a) 'Transporter binding in people who use ecstasy appears to recover with abstinence, unlike the persistent reductions reported years after fenfluramine, a drug prescribed to millions' is given as fact; in the source it is the commentary's reading of a single-time-point comparison of people currently using and people who had stopped (Lyvers, 2011, 3rd paragraph, its reference 16), and the fenfluramine facts come from its reference 14, a legal and technical book. Propose attributing and qualifying it. (b) 'In the study designed to remove confounding by other drugs, only one of 15 tests clearly differed, and only in the heavier-use subgroup' is the commentary's count; the study's tables also show four whole-group differences at p<.05 and a second difference in the heavier subgroup at the same p=.003 (non-dominant pegboard). Add that in the no side rather than leaving it to 'what neither side can show'. (c) In the editors' reading, calling the transporter difference 'well attested' goes further than this page can support: no primary imaging study has been read, the claim is downgraded for indirectness on exactly that ground, and the review itself says not every study found reductions. Propose 'reported by several groups, though no primary imaging study has yet been read for this page'.

note: The single quotation (anchor 4, Lyvers) is verbatim and exactly 15 words, within METHODS §4.5, and it is the claim's only quotation. All eight of my anchors on this claim are confirmed at the stated places except anchor 7, where the extracted text should not say 'the reviews read in this batch': the Parrott (2013) cited by Barnett and Doblin is a different paper (Human Psychopharmacology 28, 289-307).
